And I think thats true, but I think there is something else at play here. The fact that printing higher denomination bills to make cash transactions easier would basically be admitting that the dollar is losing its value. Because, printing higher denominations is really only needed if it takes A LOT of dollars/euros/pounds to buy stuff. For instance. Try to buy a brand new car with $100 bills. First of all, even if you have the cash in the bank, for a $30,000 car you're going to need 300 $100 bills. Its sort of difficult for a person to handle that much money discretely from the bank to the dealership. Then they have to count the money at the dealership. And if you manage to haggle them down by $5000, you still have a full stack of 50 $100 bills. The easier thing is to just get a cashiers check, or to take out a loan...or anything else that leaves an easily traceable paper trail. 30 years ago, that car would have maybe cost 10grand and the whole cash process would have been much easier. Preventing you from using cash is what they want. It prevents you from actually seeing, in physical form, the amount of money you're paying for something. Because if you can't see it, you're going to spend it more freely.
